passage: Uma's mother, Jaya, had stitched blouses for fifteen years to pay for her daughter's engineering degree, and the whole street knew the dream: Uma would become a bank manager. Now the offer letter from the bank lay on the dining table beside the tea. But that month Uma had also been helping a small group build science kits for village schools, and she came home humming. At dinner she took a breath. "Amma, I'm grateful for everything. I'll take the bank job, and I want to keep working on the kits on weekends. Can we talk about what I can give the house each month?" Jaya put down her roti and said nothing for a while. Then, "I only wanted you to never need anyone." Uma reached for her hand. They talked until the dal went cold.

qa.q: For how many years had Jaya stitched blouses?
qa.a: Jaya had stitched blouses for fifteen years to pay for her daughter's engineering degree.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling and wanting as she took a breath at dinner?
qa.a: Uma felt grateful but also wanted her own kit project to have a place in her life, so she nervously asked to talk openly about both.

qa.q: What could Uma and Jaya do next?
qa.a: Keep talking honestly about what Uma can give the household each month and how the weekend kits can fit beside the bank job, looking for where duty and desire overlap.

qa.q: Why might Jaya have gone quiet when Uma spoke?
qa.a: Jaya may have heard her years of sacrifice being weighed against a new plan, and her line about wanting Uma never to need anyone shows the fear behind her dream.

grounding: Uma feels duty to repay her mother's sacrifice, is grateful, and talks honestly about what she can give and what she also wants.

passage: Sunday, 9:40 p.m. Third Sunday at the basti reading corner. I arrived with a plan to teach fractions using pizza charts, and Jasleen, the ten-year-old who always sits in front, said, "Alka didi, nobody eats pizza here. Can we use rotis?" I laughed and redid the lesson on the spot. Then I asked the kids what they wanted from Sundays. Half of them wanted help with English homework, not my charts. I felt a bit deflated, then realised I had never asked before. I almost posted a photo of the class tonight, then stopped. The kids didn't ask to be my content. Next Sunday: English worksheets and one chapter of a storybook. Small, and every week. Tired but good.

qa.q: What did Jasleen suggest using instead of pizza charts?
qa.a: Jasleen suggested using rotis.

qa.q: Why did Alka decide not to post the photo of the class?
qa.a: Alka realised the children had not asked to become content, and did not want the teaching to turn into showing off.

qa.q: What change did Alka plan for next Sunday, and why?
qa.a: English worksheets and a storybook chapter, because the children said that was what they needed and Alka had not asked them before.

qa.q: How might the children see the fraction lesson with pizza charts?
qa.a: It may seem like something from outside their lives, since Jasleen pointed out nobody there eats pizza, though they seemed glad to be asked what they wanted.

grounding: Alka volunteers small and consistently, listens to what the children need instead of imposing a plan, and avoids showing off the service.

passage: The power went out just as Jahnavi reached Rafiq Uncle's verandah, and monsoon rain drummed on the tin roof. She had come to interview the retired postman for a college alumni booklet, but his neighbours had been telling her for weeks how he carried packets of medicine to old people on his route and never took a rupee. By candlelight she skipped her list of awards, which he did not have, and asked, "Is there anything you'd do differently?" Rafiq was quiet, stirring his tea. "I missed my daughter's school plays because the route came first," he said. "The route was worth it. So were the plays." Jahnavi put her pen down. The rain did not stop, and neither did the conversation.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say he missed because the route came first?
qa.a: He said he missed his daughter's school plays.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi be feeling when she puts her pen down?
qa.a: She seems moved and more interested in listening than recording, having asked about regrets rather than awards.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do with what Rafiq told her?
qa.a: She could write about his everyday kindness and his honest regret in the booklet, letting his daily choices rather than honours show what he leaves behind.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see being asked about regrets instead of awards?
qa.a: He may feel he is being invited to be honest rather than praised, which could be why he spoke of both the worth of the route and what it cost him.

grounding: Jahnavi admires an elder who lived simply and helped many and asks about his choices and regrets, in a power cut during the rain.

passage:
Monday: Afreen scrolled through her college group chat. Three friends had announced fellowships, and one had started an organisation. She closed the phone, chest tight. "Everyone knows what they're meant to do except me," she told her flatmate Jagdish. He shrugged. "You spent all Sunday explaining pivot tables to the whole floor. You were smiling."

Thursday: Afreen kept avoiding the group chat. At midnight, with no one asking, she wrote the small tutorial on spreadsheet shortcuts she had been thinking about for weeks.

Following Tuesday: A stranger commented on the tutorial: "This saved me an hour." Afreen did not feel chosen for anything grand. She felt curious and wanted to write the next one. The group chat pinged. She let it ping.

qa.q: What did Afreen write at midnight on Thursday?
qa.a: She wrote a small tutorial on spreadsheet shortcuts.

qa.q: How was Afreen feeling on Monday after seeing the group chat?
qa.a: Her chest was tight and she felt everyone else knew their calling but she did not, which points to anxiety and comparison.

qa.q: What helped Afreen get her calm back?
qa.a: Doing work she found worth doing, like the tutorial, without anyone watching, instead of waiting for a calling to appear. 😊

qa.q: How does Jagdish see Afreen's situation?
qa.a: Jagdish notices that Afreen already spends time on something enjoyable and useful, pivot tables, and points to it, showing that purpose can be seen in what she does.

grounding: Peers seem to have clear callings; Afreen's comparison steals her calm until she does work she finds worth doing without an audience.

passage: Chinmay, twenty-five, had one free hour on Sunday mornings and forty-two flats to persuade. At the last meeting the society committee had laughed off his idea of separate bins for wet and dry waste: "Nobody will follow it." Chinmay gave no speech about the planet. He put two labelled bins outside his own door and stood beside them each Sunday. Eshaan, a nine-year-old from the third floor, started dropping the family's waste there without being asked, then checked whether the neighbours did the same. By the fourth Sunday, six flats had joined. "I'm not trying to fix everything," Chinmay told the watchman, "just this building, so children like Eshaan inherit something tidy."

qa.q: How many flats did Chinmay have to persuade, and how much free time did he have?
qa.a: He had forty-two flats to persuade and one free hour on Sunday mornings.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's remark to the watchman suggest he wants?
qa.a: He hoped to leave something tidy for children like Eshaan, aiming at one building rather than the whole world.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay's approach gain support where the committee doubted it?
qa.a: He acted locally and steadily, keeping labelled bins outside his door and standing beside them each Sunday, so neighbours could see the habit, and six flats joined by the fourth Sunday.

qa.q: How might the committee have seen Chinmay's idea at first?
qa.a: They said nobody would follow it, so they probably saw extra work with little chance of success, until neighbours began joining.

grounding: Chinmay thinks of what he leaves to children, picks one local area, acts steadily and lives it, with little time and a doubtful committee.

passage: The third time Ishita sent a client email without the attachment, I felt my jaw tighten. Then I remembered my own first month, when I sent a quote to the wrong client and hid in the pantry. So I didn't say "again?" I said, "Let's make a checklist together, and you tell me what could go wrong." I explained why the attachment matters: the client reads it first, and an email without it looks careless even when it isn't. The next week Ishita caught it half a second before pressing send and grinned at me across the desk. I'm Aditi, three years senior. Not a genius, just someone who already made those mistakes.

qa.q: How many times had Ishita sent a client email without the attachment when Aditi's jaw tightened?
qa.a: It was the third time.

qa.q: Why did Aditi say "Let's make a checklist together" instead of "again?"
qa.a: Aditi remembered sending a quote to the wrong client in the first month and hiding in the pantry, so chose patience over annoyance.

qa.q: How did Aditi's approach let Ishita learn safely?
qa.a: Aditi explained why the attachment matters and built a checklist together, so Ishita could catch the error independently the next week.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt if Aditi had just said "again?"
qa.a: Ishita might have felt embarrassed or defensive and focused on avoiding blame rather than understanding why the attachment matters. 🙂

grounding: A junior repeats mistakes the mentor once made; Aditi remembers the mentor's own learning curve, explains reasons and lets the junior catch the error.

passage: I sit across from Keerthana, so I saw the whole thing. Meera, the junior Keerthana had trained since July, presented the quarterly plan to the director on Friday, and Meera's slides had a section Keerthana had never seen. Keerthana didn't interrupt once. Afterwards there was applause, and Keerthana clapped hardest. When the director asked, "Who taught you this?", Keerthana looked at her notebook. Later she said, "Sahil, look, that was Meera's own idea, not mine," and smiled, though she went quiet while packing up. I can't know what she was thinking. Proud, obviously. Maybe a bit sad too? Next morning she moved her chair back from Meera's desk, just a little.

qa.q: Who did Meera present the quarterly plan to?
qa.a: Meera presented the quarterly plan to the director on Friday.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling when she looked at her notebook after the director's question?
qa.a: Possibly pride mixed with a little wistfulness. Sahil can't be sure, but Keerthana clapped hardest, credited Meera's idea and went quiet while packing up. 🙂

qa.q: How could Keerthana keep supporting Meera without claiming credit?
qa.a: By continuing to celebrate Meera's ideas and stepping back gradually, as with the chair moved away, rather than attaching her own name to the work.

qa.q: How might Meera see Keerthana's silence during the presentation?
qa.a: Meera may have felt trusted to present on her own, which is why the applause and Keerthana's clapping would matter to her.

grounding: A mentor watches her mentee surpass her; she is proud and slightly wistful, credits the mentee, and begins stepping back.

passage: Noor noticed that Thomas, the new junior designer, had started carrying the same green notebook she did, drinking her kind of black tea, and even ending emails with her habit of "Let me know if this works". It amused her, and it also made her uneasy. On Thursday, Thomas asked how she had got such a clean client sign-off. Noor hesitated. "That one nearly fell apart," she said. "I missed two deadlines and hid it for a week before telling my boss. I wouldn't do it that way again." Thomas blinked. "I thought you never messed up." "I mess up a lot," Noor said. "Take the parts of me worth copying, not that part." Thomas wrote something in the green notebook.

qa.q: What did Thomas start carrying that matched Noor's?
qa.a: Thomas started carrying the same green notebook as Noor.

qa.q: Why did Noor feel both amused and uneasy about Thomas copying her?
qa.a: It was flattering but also a responsibility, since Thomas might copy her bad habits and see her as someone who never makes mistakes.

qa.q: How did Noor handle being looked up to?
qa.a: She told the truth about how the sign-off nearly fell apart, including the missed deadlines and hiding it, instead of letting Thomas admire a spotless image.

qa.q: What might Thomas have believed about Noor before that talk?
qa.a: That Noor never made mistakes, as the surprise in "I thought you never messed up" suggests.

grounding: A younger colleague copies Noor's habits; she treats it as an honour and responsibility and is honest about her failure.

passage: By the fifth week, Chetan was messaging me for everything: "Saurabh bhai, which font? Email first or call? Blue or green?" 🙏 I loved being needed, honestly, and I kept answering. Then one night at nine I was picking his chart colours and thought, this isn't mentoring, this is me doing his job slowly. So next time I asked, "What do you think, and why?" He gave two options with reasons. I said, "Both fine. Which would you defend to the client?" He picked, sent it, and the client liked it. He came to my desk grinning, not asking anything. I still get the messages. They're shorter now, and they start with "I think..."

qa.q: What did Chetan's messages ask about in the fifth week?
qa.a: They asked about the font, whether to email first or call, and blue or green.

qa.q: What did Saurabh realise on the night of picking Chetan's chart colours?
qa.a: Saurabh realised that answering everything was not mentoring but slowly doing Chetan's job, even though being needed had felt good.

qa.q: Which question changed how Chetan made decisions, and why?
qa.a: "What do you think, and why?" followed by "Which would you defend to the client?" made Chetan weigh his options and choose for himself.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel now compared with the fifth week?
qa.a: More confident, since his messages now start with "I think..." and he came grinning to Saurabh's desk without asking anything.

grounding: A mentee asks the mentor to decide everything; Saurabh asks what Chetan thinks, offers options and celebrates the independent choice.

passage:
Subject: Confession, and a small plan

Pooja,

Kabir got picked to lead the client demo on Thursday. He has been here eight months. I've been here three years, and I felt the sting straight away, a hot little thing in my chest, and then I was short with him in stand-up. 😅 Not proud of that. I stayed up half the night sulking, then got bored of sulking and admitted it: he's faster than me with the data. So today I asked Kabir to walk me through his model, and I told our manager the layout idea for the demo was his. I also signed up for the modelling course I kept postponing. It still stings a little. Tell me if I'm overdoing the noble bit.

Irfan

qa.q: How long has Kabir been at the company?
qa.a: Kabir has been there eight months.

qa.q: Why was Irfan short with Kabir in stand-up?
qa.a: Irfan felt a sting of envy in the chest after Kabir was picked to lead the demo, and it came out as sharpness.

qa.q: What steps did Irfan take after admitting the envy?
qa.a: Irfan asked Kabir to explain the model, credited Kabir to the manager for the layout idea, and signed up for the course Irfan had been postponing.

qa.q: How might Kabir have felt about Irfan's short manner in stand-up?
qa.a: Kabir may have been confused or uneasy, not knowing the reason, and may have felt more welcome once Irfan asked to learn from the model.

grounding: A talented junior progresses faster; Irfan notices the envy, then shares credit, learns from the junior and keeps building own skills.
